sections.title: The problem: reasoning that survives execution
paragraphs: This is part of my student research assistant work at TUM’s Chair of Cyber-Physical Systems, starting in October 2026, under Youran Wang and Prof. Matthias Althoff. The current agent uses GPT-6.1; archived release-specific studies below include earlier model and configuration choices.

A driving agent has to reconcile route progress, interaction with other vehicles, feasible vehicle dynamics, and a goal with spatial and temporal constraints. A plausible verbal plan is only one part of that problem: it must produce an executable next motion and respond when the traffic changes.

This project investigates a hierarchy in which a language agent chooses strategies and interprets difficult interactions, while numerical planners and native validation handle trajectories and physical execution. The experiments use CommonRoad tasks with live SUMO traffic, so surrounding vehicles evolve in response to the simulation rather than simply following a hidden prerecorded future.

sections.title: My contribution
bullets: Built the agent–environment integration: persistent sessions, structured MCP tools, planning feedback, reference-path interfaces, and explicit action/state receipts.
Developed the decision contracts between high-level reasoning, planner choice, traffic-policy labels, candidate ranking, forward prediction, and bounded automatic execution.
Implemented versioned experimental orchestration, immutable source/input manifests, per-attempt records, independent execution audits, and fresh-initial-state retests after repairs.
Built replay and diagnosis tooling that ties visible vehicle motion to candidate scores, selected trajectories, warnings, strategy changes, and recorded outcomes.
Alongside the planner, developing a Transformer with a logistic-hazard decoder to predict time to traffic-rule violations, with multi-seed validation and feature ablations.

sections.title: Architecture and control boundaries
paragraphs: The language model operates through a constrained tool interface. It can select available planning algorithms, adjust permitted objective or sampling parameters, reason about route/reference choices, and manage interaction policies. It does not directly invent steering commands or advance an unchecked trajectory.

The backend combines reactive planning with rule-based or sampled continuation candidates. It regenerates and validates motion using the current measured state. Candidate generation, ranking, forecasting, and execution are distinct stages, which makes it possible to locate a failure in the appropriate component instead of attributing every problem to the agent prompt.

In the selected-forecast development revision, the configured original objective ranks candidates first. Only the selected trajectory retains its complete native prefix and receives any missing tail needed for a three-second ego forecast. That forecast is compared with traffic occupancy in matching time intervals; constructing an extra long rollout for every candidate is not used as a substitute ranking rule.

sections.title: Causal prediction and bounded delegation
paragraphs: SPOT/SONIA supplies set-based traffic predictions from current measured actors and the public map. The system distinguishes observed positions, possible future occupancy, and checked motion prefixes. Missing forecast coverage is reported explicitly, with actors still represented by their observed identity and state.

A vehicle's wait label describes a traffic-policy relationship; it is separate from the ego vehicle's actual decision to slow, roll, stop, or approach a conflict area. Physical timing and trajectory checks still determine which movement can execute. These distinctions are important in merging, ordinary car following, and crossing traffic.

The agent can delegate a bounded interval of automatic execution, but the world is rechecked at each 0.1-second step. New hazards, stale state tokens, tracking problems, or the absence of a checked continuation return control with structured evidence. The forward-only studies disable physical rollback and replay, so an unfavorable state cannot be erased during a scored episode.

sections.title: Data, experiments, and results
paragraphs: The task data consists of road networks, vehicle initial states, reactive traffic, and CommonRoad planning goals. It is an evaluation environment rather than a dataset used to train a new end-to-end driving network. Each campaign records the source version, inputs, model configuration, budget, and every attempt.

Two completed evaluation snapshots illustrate the work's scale and the importance of release-specific reporting. The later campaign used a different language-agent/configuration and several separately frozen repair revisions.

bullets: Strict success requires the native goal and validity checks, successful termination, and the independent execution/forecast audit—not merely visual progress toward the target.
Planning noncompletion, actual contact, infrastructure faults, and numerical trajectory cost are recorded separately. Results from different releases are not pooled into a best-case success rate.
The simulator pauses during language-model decisions. These studies evaluate closed-loop behavior and tooling, rather than demonstrating real-time on-road response latency.

paragraphs: My project presentation illustrates how the agent adapts its planning tools and reference path when a default continuation fails. Its v0.6.0 architecture includes a section-scoring strategy, several numerical planning options, fallback trajectories and a failure-memory path for difficult road geometry.

The presentation reports 143/143 scenes passed and includes the Augsburg-13_1 and Jena-14_4 replays below. This is a historical presentation snapshot: its architecture permits rollback and retry, which are visible in the replay annotations. sections.title: Current research and engineering focus
paragraphs: Development continues on traffic-policy reasoning, forecast completeness, timing-aware interaction, planner recovery from the current state, and reliable model/tool transport. The published selected-forecast engineering revision has its own component and tool-loading validation; it does not inherit a full-suite result from an older release.

The central capability developed here is connecting an uncertain reasoning system to a stateful physical simulator through explicit contracts, useful feedback, and reproducible experiments. Native CommonRoad, SUMO, planner, and SPOT/SONIA components remain credited foundations; my work is the agentic integration and the execution/evaluation machinery around them.

sections.title: Related work: neural traffic-rule prediction
paragraphs: My HiWi work also includes predicting when a traffic-rule violation may occur. A Transformer processes grouped histories of vehicle dynamics and logical robustness features, together with a road-network representation; a logistic-hazard decoder estimates the event-time distribution rather than only a yes/no label.

I am responsible for neural-network architecture design, testing and model comparison, as well as hyperparameter search. The work includes comparisons of MLP, GRU and Transformer encoders with several event-time decoders, orthogonal-array screening and Optuna TPE refinement. Multi-seed validation and feature ablations support the comparisons.

sections.title: Predict time, not only a violation label
paragraphs: A safety monitor can check whether a traffic rule is already violated. Prediction asks a different question: given the recent motion and scene, when is a violation likely to happen? Event-time modeling also needs to account for censored examples, where no violation is observed within the available interval.

This work is part of my TUM CPS HiWi role and complements the CommonRoad agentic-planning project. The neural predictor and the numerical execution checks are distinct components; this page does not imply that every experiment is already integrated into the driving agent.

sections.title: My contribution
bullets: Designed and refined the neural-network architecture, from grouped vehicle, rule-robustness and road-context encoders to temporal modeling and event-time decoding.
Implemented and tested model variants, and compared MLP, GRU and Transformer encoders with Weibull, PMF, DRSA and logistic-hazard alternatives under a shared evaluation protocol.
Designed and ran the hyperparameter-search workflow: balanced orthogonal-array screening, Optuna TPE refinement and confirmation across common random seeds.
Analyzed controlled feature ablations, checkpoint inventories and metric comparisons to explain which inputs and architectural choices supported prediction quality.

sections.title: Transformer and logistic-hazard model
paragraphs: The model groups the time-varying inputs by their meaning: logical robustness features and vehicle dynamics are encoded with their respective branches, while road segments supply environmental context. A sequence Transformer aggregates the observation history, and a logistic-hazard decoder predicts discrete event-time hazards.

The retained configuration uses an observation history of up to 32 steps, a 64-dimensional Transformer representation, two attention heads, and a road-network encoder. These describe one selected experimental configuration, rather than a universal architecture claim.

sections.title: Architecture comparison before tuning
paragraphs: The retained manuscript compares twelve encoder–decoder/objective combinations on five traffic rules and five random seeds. Parameter budgets are kept close to 40 K, so the comparison examines representation and event-time modeling rather than simply increasing network size.

Transformer–Logistic-Hazard has the lowest combined validation rank in that comparison. Transformer–Weibull is close, and other variants lead individual metrics. I therefore compare discrimination, calibration and event-horizon precision together instead of choosing a network from one favorable score.

sections.title: From architecture selection to hyperparameter search
paragraphs: After architecture selection, I searched ten factors covering optimization, regularization, the feature encoders, fusion width, Transformer capacity, attention heads and decoder width. The retained search record uses 567 orthogonal-array configurations for balanced screening and 120 additional Optuna TPE configurations for adaptive refinement.

Screening and refinement use two seeds; the shortlists proceed to confirmation with five common seeds. Checkpoint and configuration selection use validation data, with the independent test split kept out of the search. The selected settings are then held fixed for feature ablations.

The November manuscript snapshot reports a mean validation AUC of 0.9748 ± 0.0013, integrated Brier score of 0.0315 ± 0.0006 and average precision of 0.9505 ± 0.0020 for the selected configuration. Each seed is first averaged across the five rules; the reported variation is the sample standard deviation across the five seeds. These are validation results after tuning.

figures.alt: Architecture comparison, orthogonal-array screening, TPE refinement and five-seed confirmation
figures.caption: Study workflow redrawn from the retained architecture-comparison and search records. The five-rule selection study is separate from the six-rule feature-ablation inventory.

sections.title: Data and validation
paragraphs: The broader workflow uses highD, inD, and MONA traffic data. Temporal histories and traffic-rule robustness features are prepared for event prediction; data-source and rule-specific configurations determine the concrete split and endpoint.

The retained ablation study fixes a selected model configuration and compares six rules under nine feature settings and five common seeds. All 270 selected checkpoints are indexed. AUC, integrated Brier score, and rule-aware average precision are used to inspect discrimination and time-dependent prediction quality.

sections.title: What the feature study supports
paragraphs: In the fixed validation setup, the complete input achieved the highest overall mean composite score. Removing both logical-robustness feature groups produced the largest aggregate loss. This supports the value of rule-related history in that experiment; it does not establish a statistically significant winner for every individual rule.
The study reports seed variation and paired differences. The reported checkpoints and rankings are validation-based, and no independent test evaluation is claimed.
